chunks: "I'd sort them along a few axes. By layer count: single-sided boards, one copper layer, are the cheapest and fine for simple products like calculators and remote controls.
Double-sided boards have copper on both faces with plated through-holes, the default for hobby and mid-complexity work.
Multilayer boards, four, six or more layers, add inner planes for power and ground and extra routing, so they give better signal integrity and EMI and higher density, at higher cost.
That's what you see in anything with fast digital or dense BGAs. By rigidity: rigid boards are standard.
Flex boards use polyimide so they can bend, great for cameras, hinges and wearables, but costlier and more delicate. Rigid-flex combines both.

By material: standard FR-4 for most things, high-Tg FR-4 for lead-free assembly, PTFE or Rogers-type laminates for RF and microwave where loss matters, ceramic for high-temperature or high-frequency, and metal-core boards, aluminium base with a thin dielectric, for LEDs and power because they conduct heat far better.
And by process: HDI with microvias and fine traces for compact designs like phones, and heavy copper for high current.
The trade is always cost versus density, performance and form factor, so I'd choose the simplest type that meets the requirements."
